generatedProse.concept-context: The common presentation errors show up across the School of Sport as much as anywhere. Reading dense slides word for word loses the audience; overrunning means the part that matters most gets rushed; a slide crammed with data splits attention from the speaker. In sport therapy and rehabilitation, that often means the clinical reasoning behind a treatment plan is lost in the overrun. Each error is fixable before the day, and the fix is usually less work, not more: fewer words on a slide, one clear image, a rehearsal to time. Spotting the error is most of the cure.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport therapy and rehabilitation students give the same case presentation on a patient's recovery to the same seminar group.

Tom has strong material but faces the screen and reads each slide aloud. The slides are full of assessment detail, the talk runs three minutes over, and the reasoning behind the rehab plan is rushed to make up time. The group follows the slides, not the speaker, and the main point is lost in the overrun. The content deserved better than its delivery.

Amara gives the same case but has checked it against the common errors. The slides are cut to prompts and one clear image, so the talk is to the audience, not the screen. It has been rehearsed to time, with a point planned to drop if needed, so the conclusion about the rehab plan lands cleanly. The group follows the reasoning, and the message stays with them.

The material was identical. Only Amara corrected the errors that would otherwise have undone it.
generatedProse.summary: Good content in the School of Sport can still be undone by a few common errors: reading the slides, overrunning, overloaded slides, and losing the audience. Each one is fixable before the day, and spotting it is most of the cure. You can now identify these errors, tell them apart from sound delivery choices, and correct them. With a fitting approach, a supporting structure and the errors in check, you are ready to deliver well.

check.body: In the worked example, what did Amara do that corrected the errors?

items.text: She cut the slides to prompts and one clear image, and rehearsed to time with a point to drop.
She added more assessment detail to the slides so nothing was forgotten.
She spoke faster to fit all the material in.
She faced the screen so the slides could be read in full.

feedback.correct: That's right. Cutting slides to prompts and a clear image, and rehearsing to time, corrected the errors.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the corrections that fixed the reading and the overrun.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara cut the slides to prompts and one image and rehearsed to time, with a point to drop. More detail, speaking faster or facing the screen are the errors, not fixes.
